findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The background cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This change affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and can substantially increase filesystem and database load. The PR description does not mention this cadence change; if it is accidental it should be reverted, and if intentional it should be justified and preferably configurable.

findings.title: Routine cleanup operations are logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log normal batch progress using Error level and include the full ids slice and a nil error. With large batch sizes (the added test uses 32767) and the cleanup ticker now running every minute, this can flood logs, produce misleading error entries, and add unnecessary CPU/log throughput. These should be Debug/Trace logs and should avoid emitting full ID lists.

findings.title: SQLite inline IN list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: deleteByIDs builds the SQLite inline IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). For large batches this copies the growing string on every iteration, causing O(n^2) allocations and CPU. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

findings.title: Only SQLite parameter limit is handled for large IN lists
findings.body: For non-SQLite databases, deleteByIDs builds a DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...) statement with one bind parameter per ID. Only SQLite is special-cased. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured larger than the placeholder/bind limit of the target database (for example MySQL or PostgreSQL limits around 65535 parameters), the DELETE can fail and halt cleanup. Consider chunking deletes into a universally safe size instead of relying solely on the SQLite check.
